common_name: Ingwersen's Variety Bigroot Cranesbill (Pale Pink Bigroot Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in average, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; Ingwersen's Variety spreads by thick surface rhizomes to form a dense weed-smothering mat and rarely needs division except to control its footprint.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil anywhere from full sun to fairly deep shade; Ingwersen's Variety is a compact selection of bigroot geranium bearing pale shell-pink flowers with darker pink calyces above aromatic, semi-evergreen foliage in late spring. Its thick surface rhizomes knit together into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover that tolerates dry shade, root competition, and neglect better than almost any other hardy geranium. Foliage often takes on rich orange-red tones in fall and persists through mild winters, and a light shearing after bloom keeps the mat neat. Established plants need little supplemental water once settled and rarely require division except to curb spread.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; A.T. Johnson forms a mounding clump and benefits from being cut back hard after the first flush to encourage a strong rebloom.

directions: Plant in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; A.T. Johnson bears an abundance of luminous silvery-pink flowers with faintly darker veining over mounded, semi-evergreen foliage from late spring well into summer. This long-established oxonianum selection is valued for its unusually pale, shimmering flower color that reads almost silver in low light, and for a vigorous, floriferous habit that fills gaps quickly in a mixed border. Shear the clump back hard by half after the main flush fades to remove tired foliage and spent flowers and prompt a strong second round of bloom into fall. Established plants tolerate summer heat and brief dry spells better than many other cranesbills.

common_name: Mrs Kendall Clark Meadow Cranesbill (Pale Lilac-Grey Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; Mrs Kendall Clark forms an upright clump and benefits from staking or the support of nearby perennials once in full flower.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to light partial shade; Mrs Kendall Clark produces unusually pale, smoky lilac-grey flowers finely veined in soft pink over deeply lobed, meadow cranesbill foliage in early to midsummer. Its subdued, opalescent flower color pairs unusually well with silver foliage and pastel companions, standing out among the more typical violet-blue pratense selections. Cut the whole clump back hard to the base immediately after the first flowering flush to tidy the sprawling foliage and often coax a lighter second bloom later in the season. It self-sows modestly and established clumps are long-lived and drought-tolerant once rooted in.

common_name: New Hampshire Purple Bloody Cranesbill (Rich Magenta-Purple Geranium)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; New Hampshire Purple forms a low, spreading mound and tolerates poor or rocky soil once established.

directions: Plant in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; New Hampshire Purple bears a long summer succession of rich magenta-purple flowers over finely cut, mounding foliage that reddens attractively in fall. Selected for its deeper, more saturated flower color than the typical species, it spreads gradually by rhizomes into a dense, weed-resistant mat useful for edging, banks, and rock gardens. It shrugs off heat, drought, and poor rocky soil once established and rarely needs staking or division. Shear lightly after the main flush to tidy the foliage and encourage continued sporadic bloom into autumn.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Patricia scrambles and sprawls, so give it room to weave through neighboring perennials or provide light support.

directions: Plant in fertile, moisture-retentive, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Patricia is a G. psilostemon hybrid bearing vivid magenta flowers with a pronounced black eye over lobed green foliage from early summer into fall. Its lax, sprawling stems scramble a considerable distance through neighboring plants, making it an effective color accent threaded among shrubs or sturdier perennials rather than grown as a tidy clump. Cut back hard after the first flush of bloom to renew the foliage and prompt continued flowering through late summer. It is generally more compact and floriferous than its parent species and tolerates a wide range of garden conditions once established.

common_name: White Mourning Widow Cranesbill (Geranium phaeum Album)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Album self-sows true from seed and naturalizes readily under trees and shrubs.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; Album bears clean white, reflexed flowers on tall wiry stems held well above mounded, softly lobed foliage in late spring. Unlike the somber near-black purple of the typical mourning widow geranium, this white-flowered form brightens shaded woodland gardens and pairs easily with almost any companion color. It self-sows readily and comes true from seed, naturalizing gently under trees and large shrubs without becoming aggressive. Cut flowering stems to the ground after bloom to tidy the clump and encourage fresh foliage for the rest of the season.
